claim: Some models suggest that dlPFC activation during normative choice reflects controlled inhibition or modulation of default hedonistic preferences.
source: Some models suggest that dlPFC activation during normative choice reflects controlled inhibition or modulation of default hedonistic preferences.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents an established theoretical perspective in the field.

claim: Evidence accumulation models predict trial-by-trial variation in dlPFC response across three fMRI paradigms and two self-control contexts (altruistic sacrifice and healthy eating).
source: Here, we develop an alternative account, showing that evidence accumulation models predict trial-by-trial variation in dlPFC response across three fMRI paradigms and two self-control contexts (altruistic sacrifice and healthy eating).
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling and empirical fMRI data presented in the manuscript across multiple datasets.

claim: Although dlPFC activity might typically increase for norm-consistent choices, deliberate self-regulation focused on normative goals should decrease or even reverse this pattern.
source: although dlPFC activity might typically increase for norm-consistent choices, deliberate self-regulation focused on normative goals should decrease or even reverse this pattern (i.e., greater dlPFC response for hedonistic, self-interested choices).
evidence: This is a novel prediction derived from the computational model simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The predictions about dlPFC activity patterns were confirmed in both altruistic and dietary choice contexts.
source: We confirmed these predictions in both altruistic and dietary choice contexts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the empirical fMRI results from Datasets 1, 2, and 3 presented in the manuscript.

claim: dlPFC response during normative choice may depend more on value-based evidence accumulation than inhibition of baser instincts.
source: Our results suggest that dlPFC response during normative choice may depend more on value-based evidence accumulation than inhibition of our baser instincts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the computational modeling and empirical results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Compared to unhealthy food choices, healthier choices in successful dieters were accompanied by greater activation in a posterior region of the dlPFC.
source: For instance, compared to unhealthy food choices, healthier choices in successful dieters were accompanied by greater activation in a posterior region of the dlPFC (Hare et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior published research.

claim: Greater dlPFC response has been observed when individuals make normatively favored choices in social decision making.
source: Greater dlPFC response in a similar region has also been observed when individuals make normatively favored choices in both social decision making (Strombach et al., 2015; Cutler and Campbell-Meiklejohn, 2019) and intertemporal choice (Luo et al., 2012; McClure et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Activation in the dlPFC increases when individuals explicitly focus on eating healthy.
source: Moreover, activation in the dlPFC increases when individuals explicitly focus on eating healthy (Hare et al., 2011a) or on decreasing craving for food (Kober et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Electrical disruption of the dlPFC decreases patience.
source: Electrical disruption of this area also decreases patience (Figner et al., 2010) and reduces normative behavior in cooperative contexts like the Ultimatum game (Ruff et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Researchers often fail to observe increased dlPFC recruitment when individuals make pro-social or intertemporally normative choices.
source: For example, researchers often fail to observe increased dlPFC recruitment when individuals make pro-social or intertemporally normative choices (Zaki and Mitchell, 2011; Tusche et al., 2016; Magen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research showing inconsistent findings.

claim: Electrical disruption of the dlPFC has been observed to decrease appetitive valuation of foods.
source: Moreover, electrical disruption of the dlPFC has been observed both to decrease appetitive valuation of foods (Camus et al., 2009) and to increase generous behavior in altruistic choice tasks like the Dictator game (Ruff et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The posterior dlPFC region associated with normative self-control success and inhibitory control tasks also activates during choices that are more difficult to discriminate in simple perceptual and value-based choices lacking a self-control conflict.
source: This account draws on prior research in both perceptual and value-based decision making, which consistently finds that the posterior dlPFC region associated with both normative 'self-control success' and inhibitory control tasks also activates during choices that are more difficult to discriminate in simple perceptual and value-based choices lacking a self-control conflict (e.g., Heekeren et al., 2004; Noppeney et al., 2010; Pedersen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The dlPFC may be one hub in a larger neural circuit that selects actions for execution using a process of evidence accumulation toward a threshold for response.
source: Our account is also inspired by findings that the dlPFC may be one hub in a larger neural circuit – encompassing additional regions like the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex [dACC], supplementary motor area, and inferior frontal gyrus/anterior insula [IFG/aIns] – that selects actions for execution using a process of evidence accumulation toward a threshold for response (Hanks et al., 2015; Hare et al., 2011b; Pisauro et al., 2017; Gluth et al., 2012; Rodriguez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The brain makes decisions through a process of value-based attribute integration and evidence accumulation.
source: Based on work examining simple perceptual and value-based choices (Milosavljevic et al., 2010; Krajbich et al., 2010; Busemeyer et al., 2019), we assume that the brain makes decisions through a process of value-based attribute integration and evidence accumulation (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Choices are resolved by accumulating information about the value of choice-relevant information (attributes), weighted by their momentary goal relevance, until a critical threshold for choice is reached.
source: More specifically, choices are resolved by accumulating information about the value of choice-relevant information (attributes), weighted by their momentary goal relevance, until a critical threshold for choice is reached.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption of the computational model presented in the manuscript.

claim: Whether a process of value-based evidence accumulation results in a hedonistic or normative choice depends not only on the magnitude of hedonic and normative attributes, but also on their weight.
source: Intuitively, whether a process of value-based evidence accumulation results in a hedonistic or normative choice depends not only on the magnitude of hedonic and normative attributes, but also on their weight: higher weights on normative attributes lead to more norm-consistent responses.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the computational model structure.

claim: Activity in the dlPFC reflects processes related to the evidence accumulation stage of decisions.
source: In contrast, we propose that activity in this region reflects processes related to the evidence accumulation stage of decisions.
evidence: This is the central theoretical proposal of the manuscript, tested through computational modeling and empirical data.

claim: dlPFC response during normative choice represents a downstream consequence of valuation processes, rather than a direct causal influence upon them.
source: This suggests that dlPFC response during normative choice represents a downstream consequence of valuation processes, rather than a direct causal influence upon them.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the computational model and its predictions.

claim: Normative choices should be associated with greater neural activation in the dlPFC only when hedonic attribute values directly oppose normative attribute values, and hedonic attributes receive more weight as inputs to the evidence accumulation process.
source: These simulations suggest that normative choices should be associated with greater neural activation in the dlPFC only when two things are true: hedonic attribute values directly oppose normative attribute values, and hedonic attributes receive more weight as inputs to the evidence accumulation process.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from computational model simulations.

claim: When normative attributes receive more weight, hedonistic choices should produce greater activity in the dlPFC.
source: In contrast, when normative attributes receive more weight, hedonistic choices should produce greater activity in the dlPFC and other areas associated with response selection.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from computational model simulations.

claim: If people by default favor hedonic over normative attributes, then most studies will observe greater dlPFC response when people choose the normatively favored option.
source: First, if people by default favor hedonic over normative attributes, then most studies will observe greater dlPFC response when people choose the normatively favored option.
evidence: This is a conditional prediction derived from the computational model.

claim: If a normally hedonistic decision maker focuses on normative goals, this should reduce activation in the dlPFC when choosing the normatively favored option.
source: However, our model makes a second, more novel prediction: if a normally hedonistic decision maker focuses on normative goals, this should reduce activation in the dlPFC when choosing the normatively favored option.
evidence: This is a novel prediction derived from the computational model.

claim: The likelihood of a normative choice depends on the value of hedonic and normative attributes.
source: Observation 1: The likelihood of a normative choice depends on the value of hedonic and normative attributes
evidence: This observation is derived from computational model simulations shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A decision maker tends to choose more healthily when one option dominates on both healthiness and tastiness (no-conflict trials).
source: As can be seen, the magnitude and sign of the two attributes matter: she tends to choose more healthily when one option dominates on both healthiness and tastiness (no-conflict trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A decision maker chooses less healthily when one option is tastier while the other is healthier (conflict trials).
source: She chooses less healthily when one option is tastier while the other is healthier (conflict trials).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: A decision maker is least likely to choose normatively when the difference in tastiness is large, and the difference in healthiness is small.
source: She is least likely to choose normatively when the difference in tastiness is large, and the difference in healthiness is small.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The likelihood of a normative choice depends on weights given to normative and hedonic attributes.
source: Observation 2: The likelihood of a normative choice depends on weights given to normative and hedonic attributes
evidence: This observation is derived from computational model simulations shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: The decision maker chooses healthily less frequently when the weight on tastiness is higher than weight on healthiness.
source: Unsurprisingly, the decision maker chooses healthily less frequently when the weight on tastiness is higher than weight on healthiness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2b-c.

claim: Differences in healthy choice frequency based on attribute weights are starkest in conflict trials, and essentially vanish for no-conflict trials.
source: However, these differences are starkest in conflict trials, and essentially vanish for no-conflict trials (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2c.

claim: When options do not conflict on healthiness or tastiness, healthy choices generally elicit less activity than unhealthy ones.
source: First, when options do not conflict on healthiness or tastiness (i.e., one option is better on both), healthy choices generally elicit less activity than unhealthy ones (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: For no-conflict trials, healthy choices elicit less neural activity than unhealthy ones irrespective of whether a decision maker is currently prioritizing tastiness or healthiness.
source: Notably, for no-conflict trials, this holds true irrespective of whether a decision maker is currently prioritizing tastiness or healthiness.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: When attributes conflict, neural activity during healthy vs. unhealthy choices shows a striking dependence on an individual's goals.
source: Second, and more importantly, when attributes conflict, neural activity during healthy vs. unhealthy choices shows a striking dependence on an individual's goals (i.e., the relative balance of wHealth and wTaste).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: In conflict trials, hedonism-favoring goals result in higher activity on average when choosing healthily.
source: In conflict trials, hedonism-favoring goals (i.e., wTaste > wHealth) result in higher activity on average when choosing healthily.
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: When goals prioritize normative attributes like healthiness, simulated neural responses are lower on average for healthy compared to unhealthy choices.
source: In contrast, when goals prioritize normative attributes like healthiness (i.e., wHealth > wTaste), simulated neural responses are lower on average for healthy compared to unhealthy choices (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The neural response is positively associated with normative choice only when the decision maker places a higher weight on hedonistic than normative attributes.
source: Thus, the neural response is positively associated with normative choice (i.e., greater neural activity to choose normatively instead of hedonistically) only when the decision maker places a higher weight on hedonistic than normative attributes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 2d.

claim: At least one region of the dlPFC correlates with evidence accumulation signals in simple choice.
source: Preliminary evidence suggests that at least one region of the dlPFC correlates with evidence accumulation signals in simple choice (Hare et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Trial-by-trial simulated neural activity in the DDM correlated with activity in the dlPFC region associated with inhibition and self-control across different choice contexts.
source: We thus began by verifying that trial-by-trial simulated neural activity in the DDM correlated with activity in this region for complex, multi-attribute choices typical of different real-world self-control dilemmas.
evidence: This claim is supported by the empirical fMRI results from GLM 1a-c presented in the manuscript and shown in Figure 4a-c.

claim: In Dataset 1, subjects naturally placed more weight on their own outcomes than the other person's outcomes.
source: Weights from the best-fitting model parameters indicated that subjects naturally placed more weight on their own outcomes (mean wSelf=0.0043 ± 0.0011 s.d.) than the other person's outcomes (mean wOther = 0.0018 ± 0.0018, paired-t50=14.465, p<2.2 × 10–16) or on fairness (i.e., |Self – Other|, mean wFairness = 0.0011 ± 0.0032, paired-t50=7.33, p=1.829 × 10–9)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 1, a significant increase in average response in the dlPFC was observed during generous compared to selfish choices.
source: We observed a significant increase in average response during generous compared to selfish choices (paired-t43=2.13, p=0.04, Cohen's d=0.32), confirming our prediction of higher dlPFC activity for normative choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 1, individual differences in weights on other vs. self correlated negatively with differences in dlPFC BOLD response for generous vs. selfish choices.
source: Moreover, for our primary dlPFC ROI, when correlating individual differences in weights on other vs. self (i.e., wOther – wSelf) with differences in dlPFC BOLD response for generous vs. selfish choices, we observed a significant negative relationship of roughly the same magnitude as predicted by simulations (r=–0.31, p=0.04).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and model parameters.

claim: In Dataset 2, the regulatory focus manipulation yielded significantly different weights on the attributes across the conditions.
source: This analysis confirmed that our manipulation yielded significantly different weights on the attributes across the conditions (all F2,96 > 13.54, all p<6.59 × 10–6, see Methods for details of model fitting).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 2, weights for self-interest were highest in the Natural condition, lower in the Ethics condition, and lowest in the Partner condition.
source: As expected, weights for self-interest (a hedonic attribute, wSelf) were highest in the Natural condition (MNatural = 0.0073 ± 0.0035 s.d.), lower in the Ethics condition (MEthics = 0.0061 ± 0.0047), and lowest in the Partner condition (MPartner = 0.0037 ± 0.0065).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 2, weights on the partner's outcomes and fairness increased with regulation.
source: By contrast, weights on the partner's outcomes and fairness (attributes related more strongly to social norms) increased with regulation (wOther: MNatural = 0.0010 ± 0.0038, MEthics = 0.0041 ± 0.0045, MPartner = 0.0051 ± 0.0038; wFairness: MNatural = 0.0017 ± 0.0033, MEthics = 0.0053 ± 0.0046, MPartner = 0.0024 ± 0.0035)
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 2, there was a significant effect of condition on dlPFC response for generous vs. selfish choice.
source: This analysis revealed a significant effect of condition on dlPFC response (F2,96 = 5.91, p=0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 2, in the Natural condition, generous choices elicited significantly greater activity in the dlPFC than hedonic choices.
source: Post hoc planned comparisons confirmed that in the Natural condition, generous choices elicited significantly greater activity in the dlPFC than hedonic choices (t48=2.16, p=0.04, Cohen's d=0.31, Figure 4h), replicating the observed difference during Natural choices of Study 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: In Dataset 2, in the Ethics and Partner focus conditions, generous choices no longer elicited significantly greater activation in the dlPFC.
source: By contrast, in the Ethics and Partner focus conditions, generous choices no longer elicited significantly greater activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 2, the difference in activation between generous vs. selfish choice in both the Partner and Ethics conditions differed significantly from the difference in the Natural condition.
source: However, the key test of our predictions was confirmed: the difference in activation between generous vs. selfish choice in both the Partner and Ethics conditions differed significantly from the difference in the Natural condition (G vs. S, Partner vs. Natural: t48=2.57, p=0.01, Cohen's d=0.36; G vs. S, Ethics vs. Natural: t48=3.13, p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.45).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 3, the regulatory manipulation yielded significantly different weights on the different attributes across the conditions.
source: This analysis confirmed that our manipulation yielded significantly different weights on the different attributes across the conditions (all F2,220 > 44.43, all p<2.2 × 10–16).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 3, weights on tastiness were highest in the Taste and Natural conditions, and lowest in the Health condition.
source: As expected, weights on tastiness (a hedonic attribute) were highest in the Taste and Natural conditions (MTaste = 0.0056 ± 0.0043, MNatural = 0.0058 ± 0.0036), and lowest in the Health condition (MHealth = 0.0027 ± 0.0033).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 3, weights on healthiness were lowest in the Taste condition, similar though slightly higher in the Natural condition, and highest in the Health condition.
source: Weights on healthiness (a normative attribute) showed the opposite pattern, being lowest in the Taste condition (MTaste = 0.0002 ± 0.0022), similar though slightly higher in the Natural condition (MNatural = 0.0005 ± 0.0021), and highest in the Health condition (MHealth = 0.0042 ± 0.0035).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of model parameters fitted to behavioral data.

claim: In Dataset 3, there was a significant effect of condition on dlPFC response for healthy vs. unhealthy choice in conflict trials.
source: As predicted by the simulations (Figure 4f), this analysis revealed a significant effect of condition on dlPFC response (F2,177 = 4.11, p=0.02).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 3, BOLD response during healthy compared to unhealthy choices was significantly greater in the Natural condition for the dlPFC.
source: BOLD response during healthy compared to unhealthy choices was significantly greater in the Natural condition for the dlPFC (paired-t100=2.35, p=0.02, Cohen's d=0.24, within-condition comparison).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 3, in the Health condition, healthy vs. unhealthy choices elicited comparable dlPFC responses.
source: As predicted, in the Health condition, healthy vs. unhealthy choices elicited comparable dlPFC responses (paired-t97=0.86, p=0.39, Cohen's d=0.09, within-condition comparison) and even showed a trend toward greater activity for unhealthy choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 3, the reduction of the difference in activity during healthy vs. unhealthy choices between Natural and Health conditions was significant.
source: Importantly, the reduction of the difference in activity during healthy vs. unhealthy choices between Natural and Health conditions was significant (paired-t93=2.58, p=0.01, Cohen's d=0.27).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: In Dataset 3, when examining only non-conflict trials, there was no significant influence of regulatory condition on the difference in neural activity between healthy and unhealthy choice.
source: As predicted, when examining only non-conflict trials, there was no significant influence of regulatory condition on the difference in neural activity between healthy and unhealthy choice (F2,213 = 0.357, p=0.7).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Activation in the dlPFC for normative choices when normative and hedonic attributes did not conflict is generally low, and shows no significant effect of regulatory focus.
source: In other words, as expected from model simulations (Figure 2d), activation in the dlPFC for normative choices when normative and hedonic attributes did not conflict is generally low, and shows no significant effect of regulatory focus.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of fMRI data and comparison to model predictions.

claim: The 'prepotent response' may correspond to choices consistent with the choice attribute that is currently receiving higher weight, regardless of the source of that weight.
source: Instead, our model suggests that the 'prepotent response' may correspond, at least in the realm of value-based decision making, to choices consistent with the choice attribute that is currently receiving higher weight, regardless of the source of that weight.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results in the context of existing theories.

claim: Even when higher weights on normative attributes derive primarily from a deliberative, regulatory focus, this yields reduced activity in the dlPFC when making normative choices.
source: In other words, even when higher weights on normative attributes derive primarily from a deliberative, regulatory focus, as in our final two datasets (Hare et al., 2011a; Tusche and Hutcherson, 2018; Schmidt et al., 2018), this yields reduced activity in the dlPFC when making normative choices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the empirical results from Datasets 2 and 3.

claim: Higher weights on normative attributes reduce the computation required for neural accumulation signals to trigger a normative response.
source: Mechanistically, these patterns result from the fact that higher weights on normative attributes reduce the computation required for neural accumulation signals to trigger a normative response.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation derived from the computational model.

claim: Manipulations that increase the weight on normative attributes should both promote normative behavior and make it easier to accomplish.
source: Thus, while virtuous choices associated with successful self-control may sometimes recruit the posterior dlPFC, manipulations that increase the weight on normative attributes, either by making it more salient in the exogenous environment or focusing endogenous attention toward it, should both promote normative behavior and make it easier to accomplish.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the computational model and empirical results.

claim: In the domain of intertemporal choice, the model predicts that making future outcomes more salient should amplify their weight in the choice process, promoting patience while decreasing dlPFC activation.
source: For example, in the domain of intertemporal choice, our model predicts that making future outcomes more salient should amplify their weight in the choice process, promoting patience while decreasing dlPFC activation.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the computational model applied to a different domain.

claim: Making future outcomes more salient promotes patience while decreasing dlPFC activation, which is exactly what is observed empirically.
source: This is exactly what is observed empirically (Magen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The region of dlPFC that correlated with the DDM is nearly identical to areas previously found when dieters made healthy compared to unhealthy choices.
source: The region of dlPFC that correlated with the DDM in our datasets is nearly identical to areas previously found when dieters made healthy compared to unhealthy choices (Hare et al., 2009), and when participants were required to recompute values based on contextual information (Rudorf and Hare, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current results to prior published research.

claim: The dlPFC region examined in this study appeared to correlate with the evidence accumulation stage of decisions, rather than with the evidence construction stage.
source: Instead, this region appeared to correlate with the evidence accumulation stage of decisions, rather than with the evidence construction stage, responding during decision conflict generally, regardless of whether that conflict derived from greater weighting of hedonic or normative attributes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results based on the computational model and empirical data.

claim: The evidence accumulation-related dlPFC region lies posterior and dorsal to another dlPFC area that tracks hedonistic and normative attributes in a goal-consistent manner.
source: The evidence accumulation-related dlPFC region in this study, which also corresponds to the area identified by the meta-analytic 'inhibitory control', lies posterior and dorsal to another dlPFC area that we have observed, in these same datasets, to track hedonistic and normative attributes in a goal-consistent manner and to serve as a candidate for mediating regulation-induced changes (Tusche and Hutcherson, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison to results from prior analysis of the same datasets.

claim: Gray matter volume in a more anterior dlPFC area, but not in the posterior dlPFC region identified here, correlates with regulatory success.
source: Furthermore, gray matter volume in this more anterior dlPFC area, but not in the posterior dlPFC region identified here, correlates with regulatory success (Schmidt et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Some areas of the dlPFC may play an important role in promoting self-regulation and normative behavior by altering attribute weights in decision value, but they are anatomically and computationally distinct from the region of the posterior dlPFC sometimes assumed to serve this role.
source: Thus, while some areas of the dlPFC may indeed play an important role in promoting self-regulation and normative behavior by altering attribute weights in decision value, we suspect that they are anatomically and computationally distinct from the region of the posterior dlPFC sometimes assumed to serve this role.
evidence: This is an interpretation and synthesis of the current results with prior research.

claim: The dlPFC has been associated with many computational functions and roles, not all of which are mutually incompatible.
source: While this hypothesis is consistent with results from single-cell recordings (Hanks et al., 2015; Hunt et al., 2018), we also acknowledge that the dlPFC has been associated with many computational functions and roles, not all of which are mutually incompatible.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the complexity of dlPFC function based on prior literature.

claim: It is possible that the dlPFC region observed here performs some sort of process that is correlated with, but not identical to, the neuronal computations of the DDM.
source: Thus, it is possible that the dlPFC region observed here performs some sort of process that is correlated with, but not identical to, the neuronal computations of the DDM.
evidence: This is a cautious interpretation acknowledging alternative explanations.
